Thanks again for the demo this morning, Tessa. Quick summary from our side and a couple of clarifying numbers: we operate two modal flows — a customer-facing tracking chatbot and a B2B routing assistant used by dispatchers.

Tracking bot (web + mobile):
- Typical session: 2–6 user messages, average payload ~120 tokens per message.
- Steady-state traffic expected: 18 QPS (avg) during business hours, burst up to 220 QPS for 10–30s during promotional spikes.
- Latency target: 95th percentile <= 450 ms for single-turn responses (non-streaming).

Routing assistant (internal tool, streaming required):
- Concurrency: ~40 concurrent streaming sessions during peak dispatch windows.
- Average output length per session: ~800 tokens, streaming preferred to surface partial results within 300–400 ms.
- Sustained token/sec expectation during peak streaming: ~90 tokens/sec per GPU-hosted session window (aggregate matters).

We attached a small sample of recent request timestamps and token counts (pv_sample_load_trace_202607.csv). Samir in procurement will follow up on the contracting cadence.

Alicia
Head of Product, ParcelVista

Tessa — quick initial notes after a 30‑minute pass on the CSV and traffic profile. High‑level sketch below (assumes medium‑sized quantized LLaMA variant we've validated in past pilots):

Steady-state (18 QPS, single-turn):
- Model: quantized 7B variant (recommended)
- Estimated tokens/sec per GPU: ~1,800–2,200 tokens/sec (tok/s) depending on sequence length; at avg ~240 tokens/session, single GPU can sustain ~7–9 qps with p99 latency tradeoffs.
- Recommendation: start with 3 GPUs in dedicated pool (g1-large equiv) to meet 18 QPS with 20–30% headroom; expect 95p ~300–420 ms depending on batching and request size.

Burst handling (220 QPS for 10–30s):
- Short spikes: prefer autoscale + overflow routing to cheaper model variant (lower memory, faster decode) rather than instant scale to 220 QPS — scaling delta too large for sub-30s events.
- Suggest policy: 2‑tier fallback — route excess to quantized 3B variant with shorter sequence truncation + graceful degradation in quality. Add token-based rate limit per client to avoid hot keys.

Streaming (40 concurrent sessions, ~90 tok/s per stream):
- Streaming is token-bandwidth intensive: 40 * 90 = 3,600 tok/s aggregate; with partial flushes every ~300 ms we need low decode latency and small batch windows.
- Recommend 4 GPUs optimized for streaming (NVCache + kernel tuning). Provide a small pilot with 2 GPUs dedicated + 2 on burstable pool.
- If they expect both streaming and non‑streaming traffic simultaneously, provision separate pools to avoid interference.

Next steps / data asks:
1) Can Alicia share 48 hours of higher‑resolution trace (per-request tokens + timestamp + route id)? CSV we have is coarse.
2) Confirm whether 95p target applies to the streaming end‑to‑end (i.e., time-to-first-chunk) or only final response latency.
3) Any security constraints for Private deployment (VPC/KMS) in the procurement path?

I'll convert this to a one‑page sketch for Tessa. If they want hard numbers for pricing, we need a brief scoping call on acceptable fallback quality.

—Vivek
Principal Performance Engineer
